## The Museum of Almost

There was a door between the florist and the laundromat that Nora had never noticed before.

She was almost certain it hadn’t been there that morning. She had bought chrysanthemums on her way to the station, yellow ones with petals like small flames, and the florist had complained about the rain in exactly the same tone she used to complain about everything: briskly, and as if the universe had misunderstood her.

The door had no handle. Its paint was the green of deep water. Above it, a brass plaque read:

**MUSEUM OF ALMOST**

**Admission: Free. Please do not touch the exhibits.**

Nora stood beneath the station clock, which read 11:43. Her train had not arrived. Her suitcase contained two blouses, a book she wouldn’t finish, and the folded score she had carried from conservatory to conservatory to every apartment since.

She pushed the door open.

Inside was a long room lined with glass cases. In the first lay a bus ticket punched but never used. A key had been cut for a house that no longer existed. There was an unsent apology, a resignation letter, a receipt for a meal eaten alone on what must have been the loneliest evening in recorded history.

A man sat behind a desk near the far wall. He wore a mustard cardigan and several expressions at once.

“Sorry,” he said. “We’re usually closed, but you arrived during an interesting period.”

“Interesting?”

“Am I,” he said, “the curator of unfinished things.”

Nora looked back toward the street. The rain had stopped, but the pavement beyond the door was dark and empty, without the florist or the laundromat or the station clock.

“Those things belong to people,” she said.

“They did. They don’t anymore, strictly speaking.”

“That doesn’t make them exhibits.”

The curator shrugged. “Nothing becomes an exhibit because it deserves to be. Usually it becomes one because someone eventually runs out of ways to avoid it.”

In the next case was a red mitten. Its mate, according to the label, had been lost “in circumstances that remain unclear.”

“Or perhaps this is only a room for things people regret,” Nora said.

The curator’s face softened. “Not exactly. Some of the objects are evidence of mercy. The apology you never made because you were angry. The city you never moved to because you stayed with someone who needed you. The life you didn’t ruin.”

He rested both hands on the desk.

“An almost isn’t always a tragedy. Sometimes it is simply a road you didn’t take. There’s no shame in a person discovering they were happier on the other road, or poorer, or more peaceful, or more alive.”

“That sounds suspiciously like advice.”

“It frequently is.”

Nora moved farther into the room. There were hundreds of objects in the cases, perhaps thousands. A blank application form. A diamond earring. A hotel key from a trip that had been cancelled before departure. A recipe for lemon tart with the quantity of sugar left unfilled.

Then she saw the piano exercise.

Her Chopin nocturne was beneath a glass plate in a case of its own. The paper was yellowed. At the top, in handwriting she recognized as her own, she had written *For the recital I will not give up.*

She had been twenty-two. The stage lights had shone so brightly that she couldn’t see the audience. Her hands had frozen above the keys. The silence had lasted three seconds, or three years; she had never been able to decide.

“You play?” the curator asked.

“I used to.”

He nodded as if this explained everything.

Nora touched the glass. “Does it hurt, being kept here? The things?”

“They don’t have feelings. They have histories.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

The curator considered this.

“Some of them are proud,” he said at last. “Some are relieved. And some are simply tired of being blamed for the lives that followed them.”

The station clock began to chime somewhere beyond the walls.

“Twelve,” the curator said. “Your train is arriving.”

Nora looked at the nocturne. For years she had imagined different versions of that recital. In one, she played beautifully. In another, she played badly but continued. In the worst, she walked onstage, looked at the audience, and told them the truth.

The curator made no move to encourage her.

“Most things don’t have to be completed to deserve remembrance,” he said. “And reading a piece of music doesn’t mean you have to perform it.”

The clock finished chiming. Nora left the museum without taking anything.

Outside, the train stood at the platform with its doors open. The conductor raised one hand impatiently. The florist was arranging her yellow flowers beneath a gray sky. Everything was precisely where it should have been.

Inside the train, Nora placed her suitcase on the seat. She took out the Chopin score and unfolded it across her knees.

She did not play it.

She read it.

The notes climbed and fell, difficult and bright and still requiring courage, even on paper. Some pages were worn thin. Others were untouched. She followed every bar, and when the last one ended, she discovered she had arrived without regret.

The train pulled out of the station.

In her pocket was a small brass button she did not remember picking up. She turned it over in her palm as the city slid past the window: all the florists, laundromats, missed trains, abandoned roads, and tiny unfinished things.

For once, she did not try to decide what it meant.

She simply held it.
